title: Why You Need A Student Leadership Team
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes an informal practice he uses every year: pulling three or four students with natural social influence, not necessarily the best-behaved or highest-achieving ones, into an ongoing 'leadership team' he meets with weekly. The argument is that this gives a teacher a fuller, more honest picture of the classroom than observation alone can provide, because students will only volunteer real information about bullying, confusion, or classmate concerns if the relationship is relaxed and trust has been built through consistent, fair enforcement. He is explicit that he selects for influence rather than virtue, and that this frequently means including at least one difficult or challenging student, since those students often have the most insight into what's really happening among their peers. The piece frames three recurring discussion topics -- clarity of recent lessons, interest level of current material, and concerns about classmates -- as the structure that keeps the meetings purposeful rather than a popularity exercise. Ultimately he argues the biggest payoff isn't the information gathered but that team members start acting as an informal proxy for the teacher's standards, modeling kindness and fairness during group work and on the playground.
points: Select students for influence over their peers rather than for good behavior or academic standing -- the goal is honest intelligence, not a reward club.
Deliberately include at least one difficult or challenging student, since the most insightful feedback often comes from kids with the worst campus reputations.
Structure each meeting around three fixed questions: clarity of recent lessons, interest in current topics, and concerns about classmates.
Students will only disclose real problems like bullying if the teacher has already established consistent kindness and rule enforcement.
The deeper payoff is that team members begin acting as proxies for the teacher's standards, modeling fairness and kindness even when the teacher isn't watching.
quotes: Every year, I ask three or four students with natural leadership ability to be part of my leadership team.

It’s important to mention that “leadership” doesn’t necessarily mean the best or most well-behaved students. These traits are irrelevant. I look for those with the most influence with their classmates.
Typically, this will include at least one difficult or challenging student. In fact, the most insightful input often comes from kids with the worst reputations on campus.
Yes, they will, but only if you’re consistently kind and clam and a stickler about enforcing rules. Do this and they’ll tell you everything .
There is one more benefit of having a leadership team, and it may be the most important one of all. The members of your team will start proactively using their influence for good.

They’ll naturally begin acting as your proxy, representing, modeling, and channeling your kindness, fairness, and high standards during group work, while listening to lessons, and even out on the playground.
